chapter.name: Tissues in Action
chapter.blurb: Explains what a tissue is and why plants and animals evolved different kinds of them, then works through the plant tissues that let a plant grow (meristematic) and function (permanent: protective, supporting and conducting), before turning to animal tissues -- epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous -- and finally the musculoskeletal system and the four types of joints that let bones move.

scope_in.item: Cell-to-tissue-to-organ hierarchy in multicellular organisms, unicellular organisms (amoeba) performing all functions with one cell, the definition of a tissue, and division of labour increasing efficiency
Why plant and animal tissues differ: plants mostly fixed and needing support (rigid cell wall), animals mostly mobile (no rigid wall, cells change shape), and differing modes of nutrition
The three ways plants grow (length, girth, regrowth after cutting/grazing) and the definition of meristematic tissue
Apical meristem: location at root/shoot tips, growth in length, and the onion-root activity's conclusion that roots grow only from the tip
Lateral meristem: location as a ring in the stem, growth in girth, and annual growth rings used to estimate a tree's age

Intercalary meristem: location at the base of the internode/above the node, regrowth after cutting or grazing; node and internode defined; differentiation; features of meristematic cells (thin walls, large nucleus, dense cytoplasm, little/no vacuole, tightly packed)

Permanent tissues: epidermis (protective) with cuticle, root hair and stomata; parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma (simple/supporting); xylem and phloem with their component cells (complex/conducting); the three tissue systems (dermal, ground, vascular)
Introduction to animal tissues as specialised groups of cells performing different functions
Epithelial tissue: general structure and its five functions (exchange, protection, secretion, sensory, absorption) with structure and body location for each, as in Table 3.2
Connective tissue: blood (plasma, RBCs, WBCs, platelets and their roles), bone, cartilage, tendon and ligament, and how each differs in matrix and function
Muscular tissue: skeletal muscle (voluntary), smooth muscle and cardiac muscle (involuntary), their cell structure and where each is found
Nervous tissue: the neuron and its three parts (cell body, dendrites, axon/axon terminals) and their roles in receiving, processing and transmitting messages
The musculoskeletal system: its components, functions, how muscles/tendons/bones work together to produce movement, and the skeleton's approximate share of body weight
The definition of a joint as a junction between two or more bones
The four types of joints -- ball and socket (shoulder), hinge (elbow, knee), pivot (neck/skull-backbone) and fixed (skull) -- and the movement each allows
The skeletal system: skull, vertebral column (vertebrae and cartilage discs) and rib cage (12 pairs of ribs, attachment to spine and sternum, role in breathing)

concepts.name: Tissues, and why plant and animal tissues differ
concepts.description: Cells of similar type and function group into tissues, which combine into organs, organ systems and the organism; plants and animals evolved different tissues because of how they live and feed.
concepts.idea: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together for a specific function. Multicellular life is organised as cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism, and this division of labour makes the body more efficient than a single cell doing everything.
concepts.rule: In multicellular organisms there is a hierarchy of organisation: cells of similar type performing a similar function group together to form a tissue, more than one type of tissue forms an organ, different organs form organ systems, and organ systems form an organism. In unicellular organisms such as amoeba, a single cell performs all functions of life; in multicellular organisms like plants and animals, different groups of cells perform different functions. A tissue is a group of cells (similar in structure) that work together to perform a specific function. The formation of different types of tissues leads to a division of labour, which increases the efficiency of the body and lets it carry out complex life processes. Most plants stay fixed in one place and need support, so plant cells have a rigid cell wall that gives strength and a fixed shape. Most animals can move (though a few, such as sponges, are immobile); without a rigid wall, animal cells can change shape easily, and this flexibility helps make their bodies suitable for locomotion. Plants and animals also differ in their mode of nutrition: animals have tissues that help digest food from external sources, while plants have tissues that help them use solar energy to make food through photosynthesis. Because of these differences, plants and animals evolved different specialised tissues, for example muscle tissue for movement and nervous tissue for messages in animals, and xylem to transport water/minerals and phloem to transport food in plants.
concepts.example: Muscle tissue in animals enables movement while xylem in plants transports water and minerals -- different tissues suited to each organism's way of life.

This division of labour lets a tree do more complex things efficiently than a single cell ever could.
s: Explains amoeba: one cell does everything, no tissue needed

concepts.name: Meristematic tissue and plant growth
concepts.description: Plants grow in length, in girth and by regrowing after cutting or grazing, and each kind of growth is driven by a specific meristematic tissue made of actively dividing cells.
concepts.idea: Meristematic tissue consists of small, thin-walled, densely cytoplasmic, actively dividing cells found at specific growth zones. Apical meristem lengthens roots and shoots, lateral meristem thickens stems and roots, and intercalary meristem lets grasses and similar plants regrow after being cut or grazed.
concepts.rule: Plants grow in three ways: increase in length (height of stem, depth of roots), increase in girth (thickness of stem), and regrowth after cutting branches or grazing. This growth requires actively dividing cells that together form meristematic tissue. Apical meristem is located at root and shoot tips and produces growth in length; in the onion-root activity, the root whose tip was left intact (Jar A) kept growing, while the root whose tip was cut off (Jar B) stopped growing, showing that roots grow only from their tips, which contain actively dividing cells; shoot tips too contain actively dividing cells. Lateral meristem forms a ring of actively dividing cells in the stem, producing new cells inside and outside in a concentric manner and increasing the diameter (girth) of the stem; the annual growth rings this activity produces can be counted to estimate a tree's age and the climatic conditions it grew under. Intercalary meristem is located at the base of an internode or just above a node (the point on a stem where branches or leaves arise; the internode is the stem part between two nodes); it lets plants such as grasses and hedges regrow after their tips are cut or grazed. Together, apical, lateral and intercalary meristems account for growth in length, girth and branching. Meristematic cells are small, have thin cell walls, a large and prominent nucleus, and dense cytoplasm with many organelles; vacuoles are generally absent and the cells are tightly packed with little or no intercellular space, which allows continuous and rapid cell division. Through continuous division, meristematic tissue adds new cells to the plant body; some remain meristematic while others lose the ability to divide, change in structure and function, and become specialised permanent tissue -- this process is called differentiation.
concepts.example: Cutting the tip of an onion root stops it growing further, showing that growth in length happens only from actively dividing cells at the tip (the apical meristem).

questions.q: A young stem is cut just above a node in a grass plant, and new growth is later observed arising from just below the cut, near that node. Analyse which meristematic tissue is responsible and explain why this type of regrowth would not be possible if the plant had only apical meristem.
questions.a: The new growth is due to the intercalary meristem, located at the base of the internode or just above a node, which continues to divide even after the shoot tip is removed. questions.q: Design a simple experiment, based on the method used with onion roots in this chapter, that could test whether a bamboo shoot grows in length mainly from its tip or along its entire length. Describe what you would do and what result would support each possibility.

s: Describes a workable marking/measuring method
States the result that would support growth from the tip

concepts.name: Permanent tissues in plants
concepts.description: Once meristematic cells differentiate, they become permanent tissues specialised for protection (epidermis), support (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) or conduction (xylem, phloem), which together form the plant's dermal, ground and vascular tissue systems.
concepts.idea: Permanent tissue can be simple (one cell type) or complex (more than one cell type working together). The epidermis protects; parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma support in different ways; xylem and phloem conduct water/minerals and food respectively.
concepts.rule: Permanent tissues can be simple (composed of only one type of cell) or complex (composed of more than one type of cell). Protective tissue: the epidermis forms the outermost layer of the plant body, a tightly packed single layer of flat, rectangular cells, protecting all parts of the plant; it is covered with a waxy layer of cutin called the cuticle, which reduces water loss and gives protection against injury and parasites; in roots, epidermal projections called root hair increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals; in leaves, the epidermis has pores called stomata, which help in gaseous exchange and in transpiration (evaporation of water vapour), which in turn helps pull water up through the xylem and eliminates wastes. Supporting (simple permanent) tissues are of three kinds: parenchyma consists of living cells with thin walls, loosely packed with intercellular spaces, mainly storing food and, in green parts, performing photosynthesis; in aquatic plants, specialised parenchyma forms air spaces that help the plant float. Collenchyma consists of living cells with unevenly thickened corners due to pectin deposition, giving support with flexibility so that stems and tendrils can bend without breaking. Sclerenchyma cells have thick, lignified walls, making them hard and strong; most are dead, and this tissue is found in stems, leaf veins and hard coverings such as seed coats, coconut husk and walnut shell. Conducting (complex permanent) tissues are xylem and phloem. Xylem transports water and minerals from roots to other parts and also gives the plant strength; it consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres -- xylem parenchyma is the only living component, the rest are sclerenchymatous. Phloem, mostly made of living cells, transports food from leaves to other parts; it consists of sieve tubes (long tubular cells joined end to end by perforated walls that transport food), companion cells (which regulate the sieve tube cells and monitor loading/unloading of sugars), phloem parenchyma (storing food, resin, tannins and latex) and phloem fibres (sclerenchymatous, providing strength). These tissues are organised into three tissue systems: the dermal tissue system forms the outer covering and reduces water loss; the ground tissue system forms the main body between the dermal and vascular tissues and includes parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma; the vascular tissue system consists of the conducting tissues xylem and phloem.
concepts.example: Coconut husk fibres are tough because they are made of sclerenchyma, whose thick, lignified walls make the tissue hard and strong even though most of its cells are dead.

concepts.name: Animal tissues: epithelial and connective
concepts.description: Epithelial tissue covers the body and lines its internal organs, with structure adapted to exchange, protection, secretion, sensory or absorption functions; connective tissue -- blood, bone, cartilage, tendon and ligament -- connects and supports other tissues.
concepts.idea: Different epithelial tissues are structurally adapted to their specific function and location. Connective tissues share the job of connecting and supporting the body but differ enormously in their matrix, from blood's fluid matrix to bone's rigid one.
concepts.rule: Epithelial tissue forms the outer covering of the body (skin) and also lines internal organs such as the mouth, lungs, blood vessels and intestine; it is composed of closely packed cells with very little space between them, which prevents germ entry, reduces water loss, and helps absorption, secretion and movement of substances. Different epithelial tissues are structurally adapted to different functions: exchange (a single layer of thin, flat cells, lining blood vessels and lungs, for rapid diffusion of liquids and gases), protection (many layers of cells with flat, tightly packed outer cells, in skin, mouth and oesophagus), secretion (cells specialised for producing and releasing substances, cuboidal or columnar, in salivary glands, sweat glands and stomach lining), sensory functions (specialised receptor cells with hair-like cilia, in nostrils, taste buds and inner ear), and absorption (a single layer of tall, pillar-like cells often with hair-like structures, lining the small intestine). A tissue that connects and supports other tissues is called connective tissue; blood and bone are both connective tissues but differ greatly in matrix -- watery, soft and jelly-like in blood, hard, solid and rigid in bone. Blood's matrix (plasma) makes up about 55% of its volume, with formed elements (RBCs, WBCs and platelets) making up about 45%; the red colour of blood comes from haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein in red blood cells, which live for about four months and are regularly replaced; platelets help blood clot at the site of an injury; white blood cells collect at infected areas, causing pus formation and inflammation (redness and swelling). Bone has a rigid matrix containing calcium and phosphorus compounds, giving strength, support and protection. Cartilage has a soft, jelly-like matrix, providing flexibility and cushioning the ends of bones for shock absorption. Tendons connect muscle to bone and bring about movement. Ligaments connect bone to bone, provide stability, limit movement, and help prevent dislocation.
concepts.example: A small cut bleeds, and platelets in the blood cause a clot to form, stopping the bleeding after some time.

concepts.name: Muscular and nervous tissue
concepts.description: Skeletal muscle produces voluntary movement, smooth and cardiac muscle produce involuntary movement, and nervous tissue -- made of neurons -- receives, processes and transmits messages that coordinate the body.
concepts.idea: The three muscle types differ in cell shape, nucleation and striation, matching whether their movement is voluntary or involuntary. A neuron's three parts (dendrites, cell body, axon) each handle one stage of passing a message along.
concepts.rule: Some movements are under conscious control (voluntary), such as running or lifting, and are carried out by skeletal muscles, which are attached to the skeleton and made of bundles of long, cylindrical fibres that are unbranched, multinucleate (many nuclei) and striated (showing light and dark bands). Other movements happen automatically without conscious control (involuntary), such as the movement of food in the intestine and the beating of the heart. Smooth muscles, found in organs like the stomach and intestines, have spindle-shaped cells with a single nucleus and no striations, and help in slow, continuous movements like digestion. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart; its fibres are cylindrical and branched with a single nucleus and faint striations, and it works tirelessly and rhythmically, letting the heart beat throughout life without fatigue. Nervous tissue forms the body's control and coordination network; its cells, neurons, are specialised to receive, process and transmit messages. Each neuron has three main parts: the cell body, which contains the nucleus and controls cell activities; dendrites, which receive signals from other neurons; and an axon, a long fibre that carries messages from the cell body and ends at axon terminals, which transmit the messages to other cells. The brain acts as the control centre, coordinating activities, memory and responses across the body; for example, during exercise the brain signals the heart to beat faster to meet the body's increased oxygen demand.
concepts.example: During exercise, the brain signals the heart (made of cardiac muscle) to beat faster, showing nervous tissue and muscular tissue working together.

concepts.name: Musculoskeletal system, joints and the skeletal system
concepts.description: Bones, muscles, cartilage, tendons and ligaments work together as the musculoskeletal system; the four types of joints (ball and socket, hinge, pivot, fixed) each allow a different range of movement; the skeletal system's skull, vertebral column and rib cage each protect and support the body.
concepts.idea: A joint is a junction between bones that allows movement, but muscles -- via tendons -- provide the force. Different joint shapes (ball and socket, hinge, pivot, fixed) allow different kinds and ranges of movement suited to their location.
concepts.rule: The musculoskeletal system is made up of bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons and ligaments; it helps the body stand upright, move, maintain posture and protect delicate organs, and works under the control of the nervous system. Muscles pull on bones to produce movement: they are attached to bones by tendons, and when a muscle contracts, the tendon transmits this force to the bone, producing movement at a joint. On average, the adult human skeleton makes up about 12-15% of body weight, though this varies with age, gender and body composition. A joint is a junction between two or more bones; joints allow movement but cannot move the bones on their own -- that requires muscles. There are four types of joints described in the chapter. The ball and socket joint (as in the shoulder) has the rounded top of the upper arm bone fitting into a shallow hollow of the shoulder bone, allowing forward, backward, sideways and circular movement. The hinge joint (as in the elbow and knee, where the kneecap protects the joint) bends and straightens in one direction only, like a door hinge. The pivot joint connects the skull to the backbone and allows the head to move side to side, like a doorknob turning in its socket. Fixed joints join the bones of the skull together so they cannot move, keeping the brain safe. The skeletal system is a framework of bones providing strength and protecting delicate internal organs; it includes the skull, the vertebral column (backbone/spine) and the rib cage. The vertebral column is a flexible column of small bones called vertebrae, extending from the base of the skull; a cartilage disc between each vertebra cushions and allows flexibility so the body can bend and twist without injuring the spinal cord. The rib cage is formed by 12 pairs of ribs that protect vital organs such as the heart and lungs; the ribs are attached to the spine at the back and to the sternum (breastbone) in the front, joined by flexible cartilage, which lets the rib cage expand and contract during breathing, changing the space in the chest so air can move in and out of the lungs.
concepts.example: Bending the knee uses a hinge joint (movement in one direction), while rotating the arm at the shoulder uses a ball and socket joint (movement in many directions).

This slight movement is essential for breathing, because it increases and decreases the space inside the chest, letting air move in and out of the lungs. So the rib cage has to balance being strong enough to protect the organs inside it with being flexible enough to move for breathing.
